parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what type of waves must meet and overlap for a stable pattern with fixed nodes to appear, rather than a travelling disturbance.
Hint 2: Consider what properties must be identical for the two waves to cancel perfectly at the same places, and in which directions they must be travelling.
parts.proper_answer: Two progressive waves of the same type with the same frequency, wavelength, speed and amplitude travelling in opposite directions.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture how a stationary wave is made**
Imagine two identical ripples travelling past each other on a string, one going left and one going right. Where they overlap they add together by superposition. Only if they match perfectly can the cancellations stay in the same place to give fixed nodes.

Step 2: **Match the waves and oppose the directions**
For this to work the two waves must be the same type, for example both transverse on a string, and have the same frequency (so same wavelength and speed in that medium) and ideally the same amplitude. They must be travelling in opposite directions so that interference produces fixed nodes and antinodes instead of a moving pattern.

parts.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: node as point of destructive interference
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the motion of the string at a node compared to everywhere else - what is the size of the vibration there at all times?
parts.proper_answer: A point on the stationary wave with zero amplitude where destructive interference occurs at all times.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See what happens at a node**
On a stationary wave some points swing up and down a lot and some never move at all. A node is one of those permanently still points. The two overlapping waves always arrive there in antiphase and cancel, so the resultant displacement is always zero.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Sketch one full wavelength of a stationary wave and mark on the nodes and antinodes - what fraction of a full wave fits between a node and the very next antinode?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link node-antinode distance to wavelength**
In a stationary wave, two adjacent nodes are $\lambda/2$ apart, and an antinode sits exactly halfway between them. So node to adjacent antinode is half of that:
$$\text{node to antinode} = \frac{\lambda}{4}$$

Step 2: **Calculate the wavelength**
You are given $6.0\text{ cm}$ for this distance:
$$\frac{\lambda}{4} = 6.0\text{ cm}$$
$$\lambda = 4 \times 6.0 = 24\text{ cm}$$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
key_concepts: in-phase and antiphase regions separated by nodes
hints: Hint 1: Think about how particles on opposite sides of a node move - when one side goes up, which way does the other side go, and what does that tell you about their phase?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember phase between nodes**
All particles between two adjacent nodes vibrate in phase with each other, they all go up together and down together. But a node acts like a wall for phase. Particles in the next loop, up to the next antinode, do exactly the opposite.

Step 2: **Apply to adjacent antinodes**
Two adjacent antinodes are always separated by one node. That means they are in neighbouring loops and always move in opposite directions. Opposite motion means antiphase, so the phase difference is:
$$\phi = 180^{\circ}$$
